extracted.intended_audience: taxonomists and zoologists (malacologists/poriferologists) and museum curators studying freshwater sponges (Spongillidae)
extracted.subtask_description: Morphological and biological description and diagnosis of freshwater sponge species and higher taxa (genera, subgenera, subspecies) with type citations, measurements, distribution, and habitat notes. Used to identify, compare, and delimit species from museum and field specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponge — external morphology (form, thickness, branches, texture, colour, oscula)
rubrics_metrics.description: _Sponge_ flat, lichenoid, never of great thickness, devoid of branches, dense in texture but very friable; colour brown, green, or whitish; oscula numerous, small, flat, distinctly star-shaped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors report for each species the gross habit (e.g. thin layer, cushion-like, spherical, spindle-shaped), surface characters (minutely hispid, smooth, rough), whether branches are present, texture (hard/soft/friable/compact), colour (including changes with light), and oscula (number, conspicuousness, shape such as star-shaped, circular, depressed) with examples across taxa (e.g. S. fragilis, S. bombayensis, Pectispongilla aurea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeleton — architecture (radiating and transverse fibres; reticulation; spongin amount)
rubrics_metrics.description: Skeleton with well defined radiating and transverse fibres, which are never strong but form a fairly dense network with a small amount of spongin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe whether the skeleton is regular or amorphous, presence/clarity of radiating vs transverse fibres, density/compactness, and amount/distribution of spongin (none, little, considerable). Examples: close regular network at base (S. gemina), compact reticulation with considerable spongin (S. ultima), amorphous dense skeleton (S. bombayensis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeleton-spicules — shape, surface ornamentation, curvature, pointedness, stoutness
rubrics_metrics.description: Skeleton-spicules smooth, sharply pointed, moderately stout, as a rule nearly straight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record skeleton-spicule characters (smooth vs roughened/spined, straight vs curved, sharply pointed vs obtuse/rounded, sausage-shaped vs slender) as diagnostic characters. Species examples and measured averages are used to distinguish taxa (e.g. blunt or truncated megascleres in S. indica; smooth skeleton-spicules in E. meyeni).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flesh-spicules (presence, abundance, form, ornamentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: No flesh-spicules. (Or) Flesh-spicules slender, sharply pointed, straight or curved, irregularly covered with relatively long, straight sharp spines, abundant in the dermal membrane, scarce in the substance of the sponge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether true flesh-spicules occur; when present, record their shape, length, and ornamentation and distribution (parenchyma vs dermal membrane). Presence/absence is often diagnostic (e.g. absence in many Spongilla species; plentiful in S. indica).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule-spicules — morphology (shape, spination, arrangement, ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gemmule-spicules cylindrical, blunt or abruptly pointed, nearly straight, covered with relatively stout, straight, irregular spines, which are equally distributed all over the spicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe size, shape (sausage-shaped, cylindrical, cruciform, rosette-like, needle-like, bifid/trifid), surface spination (minute, stout, irregular, comb-like), and whether spines occur at ends. Their form and arrangement (horizontal vs vertical) are central to genus- and species-level diagnoses (e.g. rotulate gemmule-spicules in Ephydatia; comb-like double rows in Pectispongilla).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule — gross structure (number/arrangement, coats, pneumatic layer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gemmules bound together in free groups of varying numbers and forming a flat layer at the base of the sponge; each gemmule small in size, surrounded by a thick cellular coat of several layers; with a relatively long and stout foraminal tubule, which projects outwards through the cellular coat...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record whether gemmules are free or adherent, solitary or grouped (pairs/twins/groups/basal layer), the nature of coats (cellular granular coat; inner chitinous coat; outer chitinoid coat), presence/absence and development of pneumatic layer, and arrangement of spicules within coats (horizontal/vertical/mosaic). These characters are repeatedly used to distinguish subspecies and genera (e.g. Stratospongilla: pneumatic layer absent; Pectispongilla: spicules in membrane parallel to surface).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule — foraminal tubule (number, length, curvature, thickening at tip)
rubrics_metrics.description: With a relatively long and stout foraminal tubule, which projects outwards through the cellular coat ... is usually curved, and is not thickened at the tip; more than one foraminal tubule sometimes present on a single gemmule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the foraminal tubule(s): whether single or multiple, short or long, straight or bent/curved, projecting through coats or opening downwards, and whether tip is thickened. Variation (short/straight and thickened in S. decipiens vs long and bent in S. calcuttana) can define subspecies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule-spicule arrangement (horizontal vs vertical vs mosaic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gemmule-spicules arranged horizontally or at the base of the cellular coat. (Elsewhere) the gemmule-spicules are arranged vertically, often in two or three concentric series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify orientation of gemmule-spicules within coats (horizontal plane, vertical, slanting, mosaic-like), and note whether they form distinct layers (inner/outer) or series. Arrangement is diagnostic for genera (e.g. parallel/mosaic in Stratospongilla; vertical concentric series in E. meyeni) and species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type specimen and repository citation
rubrics_metrics.description: TYPE.--Potts refers to the type as being in the Academy of Natural Sciences at Philadelphia. TYPE in the Indian Museum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each nominal taxon, cite the type specimen and its repository (museum), including co-types when relevant. This is required for nomenclatural certainty and comparison with other authors' material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical distribution (range, localities)
rubrics_metrics.description: GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION.--All over Europe and N. America; also in Siberia, Australia, and S. America. (For other taxa:) S. and W. India and S. Africa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide known regional distribution and specific localities or political/geographic regions where specimens were recorded; compare Holarctic vs tropical records and note range limits. Distributional data are used in taxonomic assessments and biogeographic inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitat and biology (substrate, depth, seasonality, associations)
rubrics_metrics.description: HABITAT, etc.--Growing ... on the stone sides of an artificial conduit ... The water was extremely dirty and was used for bathing purposes. (Elsewhere) usually found near the surface in shallow water; attached to the roots of floating water-plant Pistia; found during the 'rains' and the cold weather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record substrate (stones, bricks, stems, leaves, floating plants), water quality (dirty/soap-suds), depth/position (near surface, edge), seasonal occurrence (rains, cold weather, November), and associations with other organisms (Plumatella, Chironomid larvæ). Habitat notes help interpret life-history and can separate sympatric species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurements and quantitative dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Average length of skeleton-spicules 0.2046 mm. breadth 0.0172 mm; length of flesh-spicules 0.053 mm ... Length of gemmule-spicule 0.032-0.036 mm ... Diameter of gemmule 0.204-0.221 mm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide measured averages and ranges for spicule lengths and diameters (skeleton, flesh, gemmule-spicules) and gemmule diameters. Quantitative metrics are essential for distinguishing similar species and for comparing type material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic comparison with allied species
rubrics_metrics.description: The species as a species is easily distinguished from all others, its nearest ally being the N. American S. ingloriformis ... This species is closely allied to S. fragilis, from which it may be distinguished by the curious twinned arrangement of its gemmules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly compare each taxon with its closest allies, listing the characters that separate them (e.g. spicule sharpness, gemmule arrangement, presence of bubble-cells). Differential diagnoses are fundamental to justifying new taxa or subspecies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and treatment of subspecies/varieties/local races
rubrics_metrics.description: Several varieties of S. fragilis have been described in Europe and America. This local race, which is common in Calcutta, is distinguished from the typical form mainly by the shape of its skeleton-spicules ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When intraspecific variation is found, describe and name subspecies/varieties, specify diagnostic differences (often subtle spicule shape or gemmule features), and note geographic restriction. Cite authorities and type repositories for varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence/absence and character of spongin
rubrics_metrics.description: Little spongin present. (Elsewhere) a considerable amount of almost colourless spongin present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe whether spongin is absent, little, or considerable and where it occurs (binding radiating fibres, extending as delicate film). Spongin affects skeleton rigidity and is taxonomically informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bubble-cells and other parenchymal cell types
rubrics_metrics.description: The parenchyma contains numerous bubble-cells (see p. 31, fig. 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report presence/absence of bubble-cells and other distinctive cell types in the parenchyma; these microscopical characters may separate otherwise similar taxa (e.g. E. meyeni vs E. fluviatilis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of skeletal fibres (radiating vs transverse prominence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Skeleton forming a close and regular network at the base of the sponge, becoming rather more diffuse towards the external surface; the radiating and the transverse fibres both well developed, of almost equal diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note whether radiating fibres are more prominent than transverse ones, whether transverse fibres are numerous near surface, and whether a definite reticulation exists. These details characterize the overall skeletal plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oscula and pore architecture (shape, surrounding furrows, subdermal cavity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oscula numerous but minute and inconspicuous, never star-shaped. (Elsewhere) oscula circular or star-shaped, usually surrounded by radiating furrows; pores normally contained in single cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe oscula size, conspicuousness, shape (star-shaped, circular, depressed), and features such as radiating furrows or subdermal cavity. These characters are routinely recorded in species descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dermal/external membrane — adherence and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Dermal membrane adhering closely to the sponge. (Elsewhere) External membrane closely adherent to the sponge except immediately round the oscula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note whether the dermal membrane is closely adherent or loose, and whether it contains abundant spicules or flesh-spicules. The membrane may bear abundant spicules and plays a role in gemmule attachment and in characters used to separate species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour variation with light exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: The green flush sometimes seen on the surface of the typical form is due to the fact that the superficial cells of the parenchyma contain green corpuscles. ... The sponge was green where the light fell upon it, grey where it was in the shadow ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record observed colour differences correlated with exposure to light (green flush in lighted areas, grey in shadow), pigment presence in parenchyma, and how preservation (dry vs spirit) changes colour. Colour is a supplementary character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule coatings and membranes (number and composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gemmules covered by two thick chitinous membranes, in each of which there is a dense horizontal layer of spicules; no granular or cellular covering; the two chitinous coats separated by an empty space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the number of chitinous membranes (one or two), presence or absence of granular/cellular coverings, and composition (chitinoid substance). These features often differ between closely related taxa (e.g. S. bombayensis vs S. indica).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule attachment mechanism to substrate
rubrics_metrics.description: The outer coat forms a kind of mantle by means of the skirts of which the gemmule is fastened to the support of the sponge. (Elsewhere) The manner in which the gemmules ... are fastened to the solid support of the sponge must be particularly useful in enabling them to sprout ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record whether gemmules are firmly adherent via skirts/skirts of chitinous coat, fixed by secreted material, or free; note ecological implications for sprouting when water returns. This is both descriptive and functional information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus/subgenus-level diagnostic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The genus Pectispongilla: gemmule-spicules bear at either end ... a double vertical row of spines ... The genus Ephydatia is separated from Spongilla by the structure of the gemmule-spicules, which bear at either end a transverse disk with serrated or deeply notched edges ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify the characters that delimit genera and subgenera (e.g. rotulate gemmule-spicules in Ephydatia; absence/irregularity of pneumatic layer and presence of chitinous membranes in Stratospongilla). These higher-level characters are explicitly stated and used to assign species to genera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free microscleres — form and taxonomic importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The free microscleres consist as a rule of several or many shafts meeting together in several or many planes at a common centre, which is usually nodular. The free ends of these shafts often possess rudimentary rotulæ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report presence, number, and architecture of free microscleres (e.g. polyaxonal aggregates with nodular centre, monaxonic forms, or birotulate ends). Free microsclere morphology is a key genus-level character (e.g. Dosilia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule morphological variability and abnormal forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Gemmule-spicules variable in size, belonging to practically every type and exhibiting practically every abnormality possible in the genus, the majority being more or less sausage-shaped and having a roughened surface, but others being cruciform, spherical, subspherical, rosette-like, needle-like, bifid or even trifid at one extremity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document range of gemmule-spicule morphologies within species, noting common vs rare forms and their frequency. Such polymorphism may be diagnostic at species or population level and should be reported with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal persistence and developmental timing (gemmule formation and survival)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is therefore necessary to assume that the gemmules of S. bombayensis had been formed between July and October. ... In spite of its hard and compact skeleton, the sponge does not persist from one cold weather to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record timing of gemmule formation, seasonal appearance of vegetative growth, persistence or loss of sponge tissue between seasons, and whether gemmules remain viable/attached when substrate becomes dry. These life-history notes inform ecological interpretation and may separate taxa with different phenologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associations with incolæ and other organisms (overgrowths, larvae, debris tubules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dense structure of the sponge is not favourable to the presence of incolæ, but young colonies of the polyzoon Plumatella fruticosa are sometimes overgrown by it. ... I have found numerous small tubules of inorganic débris. These appear to be the work of Chironomid larvæ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note whether sponges harbor invertebrate associates, are overgrown by other sessile organisms, contain larval tubes or debris, and how sponge texture affects such associations. These observations have ecological and diagnostic importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specimen condition and preservational remarks (dry vs spirit; effect on characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: I have examined several specimens dry and in spirit; but S. ultima is the only Indian freshwater sponge, except Corvospongilla burmanica, I have not seen in a fresh condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record the condition in which specimens were examined (fresh, dry, in spirit), whether characters (colour, oscula visibility, parenchyma) are affected by preservation, and caution when comparing differently preserved material.
